about: Every number used by the start-up guide lives in this file. A fact row has a source (see 'sources'); an assumption row is our own named choice with a rationale and no source. Rows that nobody has read must have status 'needs_hand_check' on their source, and the calculator then ignores them. Checklist and struggle texts contain no digits: numbers appear only through {{row-id}} placeholders.

Paid hours per person per month
rows.rationale: 40 hours a week x 52 weeks / 12 months. It turns an hourly wage into a monthly cost. Real rotas differ; you can change staff costs later in the simulator.

rows.label: Other fixed bills (utilities, insurance, other) as a share of rent
rows.rationale: The same rough rule the simulator already uses and shows. It is our choice, not a source.

rows.label: Days open in a month
rows.rationale: The simulator's value for all three industries, so the plan and the simulator agree.

rows.label: Contingency added to the start-up cost
rows.rationale: A cushion for costs you cannot foresee. The low end borrows the SBA's 10% break-even cushion; applying it to start-up costs, and the 20% upper end, are our own choices and not from a source.

rows.label: Cash buffer, in months of running costs
rows.rationale: A rule of thumb for how long a new place can run on savings while sales build. It is our choice, not a standard. Ask an accountant.

rows.label: Marketing as a share of sales
rows.rationale: The share the simulator's industry template uses (the same rule as the four-question start). It is a typical estimate, not a sourced figure.

rows.label: Which published figures stand in for your business
rows.rationale: Cafes and bakeries use the limited-service restaurant figures; a restaurant uses the full-service figures. For pay, a cafe uses food and beverage serving workers; a restaurant or bakery uses cooks. The closest listed job is not your job, so real pay will differ.

gaps.text: No start-up total for a restaurant in the United States: the guides we found could not be opened by our checks, so we do not use them.
No start-up costs for the United Kingdom or China: we found no reliable published figures. Ask two or three local suppliers and agents for quotes.
Rent depends on your street, so outside the United States cafe and bakery guides we have no figure: use your own quote.
No ingredient-cost share outside the United States: use your own estimate (ask a supplier what the ingredients for your best-seller cost).
No alcohol-licence cost: it depends on your state or council.

No figures for insurance (except one bakery guide), utilities, accounting fees, equipment leasing, delivery-app commissions, food waste, seasons, or how long a new place takes to build up regular customers.

checklist.title: Find your premises
do: Decide what rent you can carry each month before you look at places.
Ask local commercial property agents what is available, and what a deposit and a lease usually involve where you are.
Have someone who knows leases read yours before you sign.
where_kinds: listing sites for commercial space in your area

checklist.title: Licences, permits and registration
do: Find out which licences and permits your city or council asks for before you spend on fit-out.
Ask the office that issues them how long they take.
Keep a list of renewal dates.
where_kinds: your local health or food-safety office
the office that issues business licences where you live

cant.US: We can't tell you which licences you need or what they cost: that depends on your city, county and state. Start with the SBA page, then ask your local health department.
cant.UK: We can't register your business for you. Registering a food business with your local council is free, and the official page says to do it at least {{rule-uk-register-days}} days before you start trading. That page applies to England, Northern Ireland and Wales; for Scotland, check the official guidance for Scotland.
cant.CN: We can't handle licences for you. The rule is set out in the State Administration for Market Regulation's measures on food business licensing and filing (食品经营许可和备案管理办法): catering needs a food business licence (食品经营许可). Ask your local Administration for Market Regulation office (市场监督管理局) which documents your city wants.
cant.OTHER: We can't tell you which licences apply where you live. Ask the local office that licenses food businesses.

checklist.title: Equipment
do: List what you need to make your first menu, and nothing more.
Ask dealers for new, used and leased prices side by side.
Check that your power, water and ventilation can run it.

checklist.title: Suppliers
do: Ask two or three suppliers for price lists in writing.
Find out minimum orders, delivery days and payment terms.
Taste and test before you commit.

checklist.title: Menu and pricing
do: Work out what the ingredients for each item cost.
Compare your ingredient share of sales with the published medians on this page.
Try a price change in the simulator before you print a menu.

checklist.title: Staff
do: Decide who you need for opening hours, and who is part-time.
Check the pay rules where you live before you set pay.
Compare your pay bill as a share of sales with the published figures on this page.
where_kinds: your local labour or employment office

checklist.title: Marketing
do: Start with your neighbours: a sign, a social page, a tasting.
Decide a monthly amount and stick to it for a while before judging it.
Ask every new customer how they heard of you.
where_kinds: social media and local listing sites

checklist.title: Bookkeeping and tax
do: Choose how you will register the business and pay tax.
Keep every receipt from day one.
Ask a qualified local accountant to set up simple books.

cant.US: We can't give tax advice. The SBA page says an EIN (your federal tax ID) is free to apply for, and not to use websites that charge a fee for it.
cant.UK: We can't give tax advice. The GOV.UK page explains the choice between sole trader and limited company; ask a qualified accountant what it means for you.
cant.CN: We can't give tax advice. Ask a qualified local accountant, or your local tax office (税务局).
cant.OTHER: We can't give tax advice. Ask a qualified local accountant.

checklist.title: Insurance
do: Ask a broker which cover your landlord, lender and local rules expect.
Compare at least two quotes.
Re-check cover when you add staff, equipment or delivery.
where_kinds: your trade body or local business group

cant.US: We can't tell you what cover you need or what it costs. Ask a broker.
cant.UK: We can't tell you what cover you need or what it costs. Ask a broker.
cant.CN: We can't tell you what cover you need or what it costs. Ask a broker.
cant.OTHER: We can't tell you what cover you need or what it costs. Ask a broker.

struggles.title: Cash running short
struggles.what: Bills arrive before sales build up. A place can be busy and still run out of money.
struggles.watch: Keep a cash buffer and look at it every week. The plan above shows a suggested buffer; the simulator's cash line shows what happens to it.

struggles.title: Rent that is too heavy
struggles.what: Rent is paid every month whether it is busy or quiet.
struggles.watch: Work out the customers you need to cover rent and other fixed bills before you sign. The break-even figure above does that.

struggles.title: Food waste
struggles.what: Food you prepare but do not sell is money thrown away. Bakeries feel it most because bread and cakes do not keep.
struggles.watch: Track what you throw away for the first weeks. We have no published figure for it, so ask a local supplier or a baker what is normal.

struggles.title: Staffing costs and turnover
struggles.what: Pay is usually the biggest cost after ingredients, and good people are hard to keep.
struggles.watch: Compare your pay bill with the published share of sales: {{share-us-labor-ls}} percent for limited-service places and {{share-us-labor-fs}} percent for full-service ones, from profitable to loss-making operators (United States).
struggles.watch_generic: Compare your pay bill with your sales every month, and ask other local owners what share of sales is normal for pay where you are.

struggles.title: Prices that are too low or too high
struggles.what: Prices set by guesswork can leave too little after ingredients, or push regulars away.
struggles.watch: Know your ingredient cost for each item and compare it with the published median of {{share-us-food-ls}} or {{share-us-food-fs}} percent of sales. Try a change in the simulator first.
struggles.watch_generic: Know your ingredient cost for each item, and ask a local supplier what share of sales ingredients usually take. Try a change in the simulator first.

struggles.title: Slow months
struggles.what: Sales are rarely the same every month. Weather, holidays and local events change them.
struggles.watch: Ask other owners nearby which months are quiet. The simulator does not model seasons, so plan extra cash for slow stretches yourself.

struggles.title: Many new businesses close early
struggles.what: Across all industries in the United States, most new businesses are still open a year later, but a real share are not. The source does not list food service separately.
struggles.watch: By region, {{stat-us-survival-1y}} percent of the newest group of US businesses the source reports on (all industries) were still open a year later. Treat that as context, not a forecast for you.
